NFORMATION PROVIDED BY USGS VOLCANOES: 
After nearly two months since episode 54 of lava fountaining (Aug. 25, 2026), episode 55 of Kilauea summit lava fountaining began at 3:19 a.m. HST this morning, October 17, and is ongoing.  

This is the 55th lava fountaining episode in the Kilauea summit caldera eruption in Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park that began on December 23, 2024. It occurs following weeks of intermittent spatter, low-dome fountains, and lava flows from the eruptive vent complex. The lava fountain from the north vent reached an estimated 700 feet high above the vent around 5 a.m. Hawaii Standard Time. 

The eruptive plume is reaching an estimated 25,000 feet above sea level. According to the National Weather Service, winds are blowing from the north-northeast direction, which suggests that volcanic gas emissions and volcanic material may be distributed to the south-southwest.  

Fountaining episodes typically last 12 hours or less, but ash can remain in the air for longer depending on wind and weather conditions.  

Please stay aware of hazards and rely on official updates from USGS, National Weather Service, and Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park.

Write OCVO

The Bank of Canada has held its key interest rate unchanged for about a year, but some economists expect rates to begin increasing again as early as next week — which would be the first hike in more than three years.

This comes after a recent warning from the central bank that inflation is expected to keep rising as a ripple effect of the Iran war and other factors.

Last month, the U.S. Federal Reserve hiked its key policy rate for the first time in three years, and after U.S. inflation in August topped 3.4 per cent.

Tamping down red-hot inflation is key to making life more affordable for Canadians amid the heightened cost of living — along with increasing wages and salaries — but in order to achieve this, it may mean some will end up paying more to borrow money.

Central banks usually increase their benchmark borrowing rate to help cool down inflation, which can raise costs for Canadians and businesses with products like variable rate mortgages, and some loans for cars, tuition and business.

“The trend continues to provide the BoC [Bank of Canada] with a warning that it needs to get on with tightening next week. We forecast the Bank of Canada will hike 25bps [0.25 per cent] next week,” said Derek Holt, vice president and head of Capital Markets Economics at Scotiabank in a statement on Monday.
